content: Escherichia coli, commonly referred to as E. coli, is a Gram-negative bacillus that is known to cause a variety of infections in humans. E. coli infections can be classified into several categories based on the site of infection and the pathogenic mechanism involved: 1. Enteric (Diarrheagenic) Infections: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC): This strain is associated with diarrhea, particularly in young children, and is known to disrupt the intestinal lining. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC): This strain can cause bloody diarrhea and is often linked to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition affecting the kidneys. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC): This strain produces toxins that lead to watery diarrhea, commonly referred to as traveler's diarrhea. Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC): This strain forms aggregates on the intestinal mucosa and is associated with persistent diarrhea. Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC): This strain invades intestinal cells, leading to symptoms similar to dysentery, including bloody diarrhea. Diffusely Adherent E. coli (DAEC): This strain adheres diffusely to the intestinal epithelium and is linked to diarrhea, particularly in children. 2. Uropathogenic Infections: Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC): This strain is a leading cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs), including cystitis and pyelonephritis. 3. Meningitisand Sepsis-Associated Infections: Meningitis-Associated E. coli (MNEC): This strain is implicated in neonatal meningitis and can also lead to sepsis. 4. Other Extraintestinal Infections: Extraintestinal Pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC): This group includes strains that cause infections outside the gastrointestinal tract, such as bloodstream infections, peritonitis, and abscesses. Each category of E. coli infection is associated with specific clinical presentations and pathogenic mechanisms, requiring targeted diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.
